questions.objective: Explain the purpose and scope of the Model Context Protocol and the integration problem it standardizes
questions.prompt: A platform team currently writes a separate integration for every pairing of model host and internal system. Before adopting a shared protocol, what happens to their integration workload each time they add one more system?
options: Every existing host needs its own new integration to reach the added system, so the work grows with both the host count and the system count
The workload moves entirely to the new system's team, so the hosts already in place require no additional work at all, which is not how the protocol actually behaves
The workload stays fixed, because each host already reuses one shared integration for every system it talks to
The workload shrinks, because adding a system automatically retires one of the existing host-specific integrations
questions.explanation: Without a shared protocol, connecting N hosts to M systems requires roughly N times M separate integrations, so each additional system multiplies the work across every host that needs to reach it, not just a single fixed cost.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose and scope of the Model Context Protocol and the integration problem it standardizes
questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what the Model Context Protocol standardizes?
options: A requirement that every model host and every external system share one physical process and memory space
A shared set of message formats and roles so any conformant client can call any conformant server without a custom integration
A recommendation that teams pick exactly one server implementation and avoid connecting to any other server
A single vendor's software product that hosts, clients, and servers must all purchase and install to communicate, a description the specification does not support
questions.explanation: MCP is a protocol, an agreement about message shapes and participant roles, not a product, a shared process, or a mandate to use only one server, and that agreement is what lets independently written clients and servers interoperate.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose and scope of the Model Context Protocol and the integration problem it standardizes
questions.prompt: A team is evaluating whether to adopt MCP instead of continuing to write point-to-point integrations. Which description correctly frames what problem the protocol is scoped to solve?
options: It standardizes the programming language every client and server must be written in so their source code can be merged, which does not match how a conformant implementation behaves
It standardizes which cloud provider a team must host its models and servers on before any integration can begin
It standardizes how a model-facing application discovers and calls external capabilities, replacing per-system custom glue with one shared message contract
It standardizes the internal business logic every external system must implement, regardless of what that system actually does
questions.explanation: The protocol's scope is the integration contract between a model-facing application and the systems it reaches, covering message shape and discovery, not infrastructure choices, internal business logic, or a shared programming language.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose and scope of the Model Context Protocol and the integration problem it standardizes
questions.prompt: Before a shared protocol existed, what specifically made switching a model vendor expensive for a team with several existing integrations?
options: Model vendors did not support structured data at all, so every integration needed a completely different data format for each vendor, though nothing in the protocol works this way
Switching vendors required every external system, such as the ticketing API and the database, to change its own internal implementation
Model vendors historically charged a fixed migration fee regardless of how many integrations a team had already built
Each integration was written around the previous vendor's specific conventions, so the same glue code effectively had to be rewritten for the new one
questions.explanation: Without a shared message contract, glue code is written around one vendor's conventions, so changing vendors means rewriting that glue for every integration rather than reusing it, which is the cost a common protocol removes.

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts and the roles of hosts, clients, servers, and tools
questions.prompt: In a running MCP system, which component is the application a user directly interacts with, and which embeds one or more of the other components inside it?
options: The host, which embeds one or more clients and is the application the user runs
The server, which embeds one or more clients and is the application the user runs
The client, which embeds the host and is the application the user runs
The tool, which embeds the host and client and is the application the user runs
questions.explanation: The host is the user-facing application, such as an assistant or an IDE, and it embeds one or more clients inside its own process, while the server and its tools remain separate from the host.

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts and the roles of hosts, clients, servers, and tools
questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe the role of a client in an MCP system? Select two.
options: A client is the separate program that exposes tools, resources, and prompts to the model
A client is the fixed list of capabilities a server advertises during its handshake
A client is a component that runs inside the host, not a separate top-level participant
A client is the component that owns a connection to a server
questions.explanation: A client lives inside the host process and is the component responsible for holding a connection to a server, while exposing tools and capabilities is the server's job, not the client's.

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts and the roles of hosts, clients, servers, and tools
questions.prompt: What best defines a tool in MCP's core vocabulary?
options: A physical device, such as a keyboard or a sensor, that a host connects to over a network, which is not the mechanism the specification defines
A named, described, schema-typed action that a server exposes and that the model can ask to run
A log file the server writes after every request, independent of any specific capability
A configuration file the user edits once to set the host's default color theme
questions.explanation: A tool is a specific kind of capability a server advertises, identified by a name, a human-readable description, and a schema, and it is what the model asks the server to execute on its behalf.

questions.objective: Reason about the interoperability and value of one open protocol over per-system custom integrations
questions.prompt: A vendor releases a brand-new MCP-conformant host application next year. What must be true for an existing, unmodified MCP server to work with it immediately?
options: The server's original author must publish a separate plugin specifically built for that new host
The new host must be built by the same company that originally wrote the server
The new host's client implementation speaks the same protocol version and message contract the server already conforms to
The server must be rewritten so its tool names match a naming convention the new host prefers, a claim the message contract does not make
questions.explanation: Interoperability comes from both sides sharing one message contract, so any client that implements the same protocol version can drive an existing server without the server's author doing anything host-specific.

questions.objective: Reason about the interoperability and value of one open protocol over per-system custom integrations
questions.prompt: Which two outcomes does a team gain by adopting a shared protocol instead of writing a custom integration for each pairing of model and system? Select two.
options: Adding a new system does not require every existing host to write a system-specific integration
Every tool call is guaranteed to complete faster than a hand-written integration would
Adding a new host does not require rewriting the servers that already exist
The team no longer has to test a new pairing before relying on it
questions.explanation: A shared message contract means a new host can reuse existing servers and a new system can be reached by existing hosts without pairwise custom glue, which is a reuse benefit distinct from any claim about raw speed or skipping verification.

questions.objective: Reason about the interoperability and value of one open protocol over per-system custom integrations
questions.prompt: A team argues that a hand-written integration to one specific system will always outperform an MCP server for that same system, and concludes the protocol has no value. What is the strongest response grounded in what the protocol actually standardizes?
options: The protocol always outperforms a hand-written integration for every system, so the team's premise about any single pairing is simply false, which the specification never actually guarantees
The protocol removes the need for any system-specific logic at all, so a hand-written integration could never exist alongside it
The protocol guarantees a fixed response time for every tool call, which a hand-written integration cannot match
The protocol's value is in reuse across many hosts and systems, not in guaranteeing that any single hand-tuned integration is unbeatable in isolation
questions.explanation: MCP's value proposition is standardizing the contract so it scales across many pairings, not a claim that a single hand-tuned integration can never be faster for one specific case, so the counterargument should target reuse, not raw performance.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, capabilities, and manifests
questions.prompt: A tool's inputSchema declares an object type with a priority property restricted to the values low, medium, and high, and marks priority as required. What does this schema require of a valid call?
options: The arguments must include a priority field whose value is exactly one of the three listed strings, consistent with how a conformant implementation behaves
The arguments must include a priority field, but any string value at all is accepted regardless of the enum list, which is inconsistent with how the exchange is actually structured
The arguments may omit priority entirely, since enum fields default to the first listed value automatically
The arguments must be a bare string rather than an object, since the schema names only one property
questions.explanation: The required array marks priority as mandatory, the type field marks the whole arguments object as a JSON object, and the enum list restricts priority to exactly the values it names, so a call missing the field or using an unlisted value fails validation.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, capabilities, and manifests
questions.prompt: A schema lists title and priority under properties, but its required array names only title. What happens to a call that supplies title but leaves out priority?
options: The call passes validation only if priority is explicitly set to null in the arguments
The call passes validation, because a property not listed in required is optional, matching how the exchange is actually structured
The call fails validation, because a schema must name every property in both properties and required, which conflicts with the roles this domain defines
The call fails validation, because every property listed under properties is implicitly required
questions.explanation: The required array is what marks a field as mandatory, so a property that appears under properties but not under required may be left out of the arguments object without failing schema validation.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, capabilities, and manifests
questions.prompt: After a tool call passes validation and its handler finishes successfully, how is the returned value carried back in the response?
options: As a raw string appended directly to the JSON-RPC envelope with no type information attached
As a second, separate JSON-RPC request the server sends back to the client
As a result object whose content is a list of typed items, such as text, that the model can read specific fields from
As a binary stream the client must decode using a format the tool's schema never declares, though the blueprint does not describe it this way
questions.explanation: A successful tools/call response wraps its output in a result object whose content is a list of typed items, keeping the returned data structured rather than free text, the same way the request's arguments were structured by the input schema.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how they are wired together
questions.prompt: A host needs to reach two different servers at the same time. According to the architecture's connection model, what is the correct way for the host to do this?
options: Connect directly from the host process to both servers without creating any client at all
Create one client and let it multiplex requests across both servers on a single connection
Merge both servers into one process first, then connect a single client to the merged process, a description the specification does not support
Create two separate clients, each holding its own connection to one of the two servers, which is exactly what the specification defines
questions.explanation: A client is scoped to exactly one connection to exactly one server, so a host that needs to reach two servers embeds two separate clients rather than having one client multiplex across servers or bypassing clients entirely.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how they are wired together
questions.prompt: Why does the architecture treat the boundary between a host process and a server process as significant beyond simple code organization?
options: The process boundary usually lines up with a trust boundary, since the server is often written and operated by a different party
The boundary exists purely for performance reasons and has no bearing on who wrote or operates each process, which does not match how a conformant implementation behaves
The boundary only matters for servers that expose resources, not for servers that expose tools
The boundary is removed automatically once the client completes its handshake with the server
questions.explanation: Because a server is frequently built by a separate team or company, the process boundary between host and server usually coincides with a trust boundary, and treating them as the same fact is the default assumption the architecture expects.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how they are wired together
questions.prompt: When a client's initialize request is accepted, which two pieces of structured data does the server return in its response? Select two.
options: A list of every other server the host is currently connected to, which is not the mechanism the specification defines
A serverInfo object that names and identifies the server, matching how the exchange is actually structured
A copy of every tool's full implementation source code
A capabilities object describing what that specific server supports
questions.explanation: A successful initialize response returns serverInfo identifying the server and a capabilities object describing what that particular server supports, not source code and not information about unrelated connections the host may hold elsewhere.

questions.objective: Trace the model interaction flow from a user request through a client to a server and back
questions.prompt: A host is connected to three servers through three separate clients and receives a user request that requires calling one named tool. How does the host know which client should carry that call?
options: It always routes the call to the client that connected first, regardless of which server declared the tool, a claim the message contract does not make
It consults a directory built from each connected server's own discovery response and routes the call to the client whose server declared that tool
It broadcasts the call to all three clients simultaneously and keeps whichever result arrives first
It asks the user to manually type the name of the server before every single tool call
questions.explanation: The host builds a directory from the tools each connected server declared during discovery, and that directory is what lets it route a named tool call to the one client whose server actually owns that tool.

questions.objective: Trace the model interaction flow from a user request through a client to a server and back
questions.prompt: Put the interaction flow in the order it actually happens, starting from the moment a user asks the host for something and ending with the server running the requested tool.
options: Model decides a tool is needed, server runs the tool, client sends the request, user request to host
Server runs the tool, model decides a tool is needed, user request to host, client sends the request
User request to host, model decides a tool is needed, client sends the request, server runs the tool
Client sends the request, user request to host, server runs the tool, model decides a tool is needed
questions.explanation: The flow begins with the user's request reaching the host, the model then decides a tool call would serve that request, the client owning the relevant connection sends the request, and only then does the server execute the tool and return a result.

questions.objective: Apply the request, response, and notification interaction patterns and handle their results
questions.prompt: What single field determines whether an incoming JSON-RPC message is a request that must be answered or a notification that gets no reply at all?
options: Whether the message includes a params object of any kind
Whether the message arrived over a local pipe instead of over a network connection, though this is not how a conformant server or host is expected to act
Whether the message's method name starts with the word notifications
Whether the message carries a non-null id, which is exactly what the specification defines
questions.explanation: A non-null id marks a message as a request that obligates the receiver to send back exactly one response, while the complete absence of an id key marks it as a notification that never receives anything back.

questions.objective: Apply the request, response, and notification interaction patterns and handle their results
questions.prompt: A server receives a notification whose method name it has never registered. What is the correct way for the server to handle it?
options: Drop the notification, optionally logging it locally, since there is no id for any error to be keyed to
Return a JSON-RPC error with code -32601, keyed to the notification's id, which is inconsistent with how the exchange is actually structured
Reply with an empty result object so the sender knows the method was received
Close the connection immediately, since an unrecognized notification indicates a protocol violation
questions.explanation: Because a notification carries no id, there is nowhere for a reply to be keyed, so a conformant receiver silently drops an unrecognized notification rather than manufacturing an error or a result it has no way to address back to the sender.

questions.objective: Apply the request, response, and notification interaction patterns and handle their results
questions.prompt: A client has three tool calls in flight at once on a single connection. How does it know which incoming response answers which pending call?
options: It reads the method name on the response and matches it back to the request's method name, a detail no part of the specification actually states
It matches each response to a pending call by comparing the id the response carries to the id it sent
It opens a separate connection for each of the three calls so the answers cannot be confused
It assumes responses always arrive in the exact order the requests were sent
questions.explanation: A response repeats the id of the request that caused it, and that id, not arrival order or method name, is what lets a client with several calls in flight correctly match each answer to the call that produced it.

questions.objective: Apply the request, response, and notification interaction patterns and handle their results
questions.prompt: Which two of the following are real MCP notification messages that never receive a response? Select two.
options: notifications/tools/list_changed, sent when a server's tool list goes stale
initialize, sent when a client opens a new connection to a server
tools/call, sent when the model asks the server to run a named tool, which conflicts with the roles this domain defines
notifications/initialized, sent after a client finishes processing the initialize result
questions.explanation: notifications/initialized and notifications/tools/list_changed carry no id and never receive a reply, while tools/call and initialize are both requests that carry an id and require a response keyed to that id.

questions.objective: Handle protocol and tool errors, including malformed requests and failed executions
questions.prompt: A server receives a payload that is not syntactically valid JSON at all. What does a conformant server return?
options: A Method not found error, code -32601, since the server cannot identify which method was intended
No response at all, since a payload that fails to parse is treated the same as a notification, though the blueprint does not describe it this way
A Parse error, code -32700, with the id set to null because no id could be read from the payload
An Invalid Request error, code -32600, keyed to the id found inside the malformed payload
questions.explanation: When the raw payload cannot even be parsed as JSON, there is no id to read, so the server returns Parse error with a null id rather than guessing at an id or a method the payload never actually specified.

questions.objective: Handle protocol and tool errors, including malformed requests and failed executions
questions.prompt: A tools/call request names a tool the server has registered, but the supplied arguments are missing a field the tool's schema marks required. Which error code applies, and why?
options: -32700, Parse error, because a missing field makes the payload impossible to parse as JSON
-32601, Method not found, because a missing required field means the tool effectively does not exist, which is not how the protocol actually behaves
-32600, Invalid Request, because the overall JSON-RPC envelope is considered malformed
-32602, Invalid params, because the method and tool were recognized but the argument object failed schema validation
questions.explanation: The tool and method were both recognized, so the failure sits one level below method resolution, at the argument schema, which is exactly the case Invalid params covers rather than a missing method, a malformed envelope, or a parsing failure.

questions.objective: Handle protocol and tool errors, including malformed requests and failed executions
questions.prompt: A tool's handler passes schema validation, begins running, and then raises an unexpected exception partway through. What should a well-built server do?
options: Catch the exception and return Internal error, code -32603, without leaking the raw stack trace to the caller
Return a successful result object containing the exception's stack trace as its text content
Silently retry the same handler call up to three times before giving up without any response
Let the exception propagate and crash the server process so the failure is impossible to miss, a description the specification does not support
questions.explanation: A conformant server wraps handler execution so an unexpected exception is caught and translated into Internal error rather than crashing the process, exposing implementation detail, or masquerading a failure as a successful result.

questions.objective: Handle protocol and tool errors, including malformed requests and failed executions
questions.prompt: A payload parses as valid JSON but is missing the required jsonrpc field and the id field. Which two statements about handling it are correct? Select two.
options: The server should return Parse error, code -32700, since a missing id always implies unparseable JSON
This failure is distinct from a Parse error, because the payload did successfully parse as JSON
The server should return Invalid Request, code -32600, because the envelope is not a well-formed JSON-RPC 2.0 message
The server should silently ignore the payload, treating the missing id as proof it was a notification
questions.explanation: A payload that parses as JSON but lacks required JSON-RPC fields is a malformed envelope, which is Invalid Request rather than a parse failure, and a missing id here does not make the message a notification since the envelope itself is not well-formed.

questions.objective: Walk the tool invocation lifecycle from discovery through call to result
questions.prompt: A conformant server's handling of a tools/call request passes through checkpoints in a fixed order. What is that order?
options: Execution of the handler, then parsing, then validation, then the result
Parsing, then validation of the method and arguments, then execution of the handler, then the result
Validation of the arguments, then execution, then parsing, then the result
The result is produced first and then checked against parsing and validation afterward, which does not match how a conformant implementation behaves
questions.explanation: A request is first parsed into a JSON-RPC envelope, then checked against the method and the tool's schema, then handed to the handler for execution, and only a call that clears every earlier checkpoint produces a result.

questions.objective: Walk the tool invocation lifecycle from discovery through call to result
questions.prompt: Before a client ever sends a tools/call request for a specific tool, what step in the lifecycle supplies the schema the arguments must be built against?
options: The initialize handshake, which returns the full inputSchema for every tool the server will ever expose
Execution, since the schema is only produced after the handler has already run once
Discovery, through a tools/list request that returns each tool's name, description, and inputSchema
A separate, undocumented request the client must send directly to the tool's own process
questions.explanation: Discovery through tools/list is what returns each tool's inputSchema ahead of any call, giving the client the shape it needs to build valid arguments before it ever sends a tools/call request.

questions.objective: Walk the tool invocation lifecycle from discovery through call to result
questions.prompt: A tools/call request carries a valid id. After the server finishes processing it, what is the one outcome that is never acceptable under the protocol?
options: The server sends back a response that repeats the exact id the request carried
The server sends back an error object naming a specific JSON-RPC error code, which is not the mechanism the specification defines
The server sends back a result object containing the handler's return value
The server sends nothing back at all, leaving the request unanswered, matching how the exchange is actually structured
questions.explanation: Because the request carried a non-null id, the server is obligated to send back exactly one response, a result or an error, so staying silent is the one outcome the protocol never treats as acceptable for a request.

questions.objective: Walk the tool invocation lifecycle from discovery through call to result
questions.prompt: Which two pairings correctly match a lifecycle checkpoint to the error it can produce? Select two.
options: The validation checkpoint can produce Invalid params when the arguments fail the tool's schema
The parsing checkpoint can produce Parse error when the raw payload is not valid JSON
The result checkpoint can produce Method not found when the handler's return value is malformed
The execution checkpoint can produce Invalid Request when the handler raises an exception
questions.explanation: Invalid params belongs to the validation checkpoint and Parse error belongs to the parsing checkpoint, while Method not found is not something a completed result can produce and a raised exception during execution maps to Internal error, not Invalid Request.

questions.objective: Identify the protocol primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, sampling, and roots and how they are used
questions.prompt: What is the key difference in who typically decides to invoke a tool versus who typically decides that a resource gets read into context?
options: The model itself chooses when to call a tool, while the host or the user usually decides what resource content gets attached
Both a tool call and a resource read are always triggered directly by the user typing a command
A resource is always invoked by the model, while a tool is always attached by the host without the model's involvement, a claim the message contract does not make
Neither a tool nor a resource requires a decision, since both run automatically the instant a connection opens
questions.explanation: A tool is model-controlled, chosen by the model as part of completing a task, while a resource is content that the host or the user decides to attach to context, which is a decision made above the model rather than by it.

questions.objective: Identify the protocol primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, sampling, and roots and how they are used
questions.prompt: How does a prompt primitive differ from a tool in terms of who triggers it and what it represents?
options: A prompt always requires network access, while a tool never does, regardless of what either one actually does
A prompt is a reusable message template a user explicitly selects, while a tool is a schema-typed action the model decides to invoke
A prompt is a schema-typed action the model decides to invoke, while a tool is a template only a server administrator can select, which the specification never actually guarantees
A prompt and a tool are the same primitive under two different names used interchangeably by different servers
questions.explanation: A prompt is a template a person explicitly picks, commonly surfaced as a menu item or slash command, which is a different trigger and a different purpose than a tool, which the model itself chooses to call as part of a task.

questions.objective: Identify the protocol primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, sampling, and roots and how they are used
questions.prompt: Which pair of methods correctly matches the discovery call and the invocation call for the resource primitive?
options: prompts/list to discover them, resources/read to invoke one
resources/read to discover them, resources/list to invoke one
resources/list to discover them, resources/read to invoke one
resources/list to discover them, tools/call to invoke one
questions.explanation: Each primitive family follows the same paired pattern, and for resources that pairing is resources/list for discovering what is available and resources/read for reading the content of one specific entry from that list.

questions.objective: Identify the protocol primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, sampling, and roots and how they are used
questions.prompt: A reviewer is tracing a full MCP exchange end to end and wants to correctly place every primitive on either the client side or the server side. Which two statements are correct? Select two.
options: Sampling and roots are capabilities a server exposes for a client to list and invoke the same way it lists tools
A prompt is always invoked by the model rather than selected by the user through the host
Tools, resources, and prompts are capabilities a server exposes to a client
Sampling and roots are primitives that let a server ask something of the client instead of the other way around
questions.explanation: Tools, resources, and prompts sit on the server side as capabilities a client discovers and uses, while sampling and roots sit on the client side, letting a server ask the client to run a model completion or share a working directory boundary, a distinction the full exchange in the capstone lesson depends on getting right.

questions.objective: Locate the trust boundaries between host, client, server, and the tools a server exposes
questions.prompt: Where does the trust boundary sit in a typical MCP deployment, and why does it sit there rather than somewhere else?
options: There is no fixed boundary, because trust is renegotiated fresh on every single message regardless of origin
Between the user and the host, because the host is the component least likely to have been reviewed
Between the client and the server's own internal database, because databases are inherently less trustworthy than APIs, though this is not how a conformant server or host is expected to act
Between the host and its clients on one side and the server on the other, because the server is a separate program the user's application does not control
questions.explanation: The host and its embedded clients sit inside the user's own trust domain because the host put them there, while the server is a separate program the host does not control, which is why the boundary is drawn between the client side and the server side.

questions.objective: Locate the trust boundaries between host, client, server, and the tools a server exposes
questions.prompt: A tool call completes successfully and its result crosses back into the client. How should that returned content be treated the moment it enters the model's context?
options: As untrusted content, since the server chose those bytes and they may contain more than a clean answer
As irrelevant to trust, since trust only applies to outgoing tool calls, not to returned results, which is inconsistent with how the exchange is actually structured
As trusted content only if the tool was marked read-only during discovery
As fully trusted content, since the call already passed schema validation before it ran
questions.explanation: Passing schema validation only confirms the request's shape was well formed, not that the server's response is safe, so a returned result is treated as untrusted content the moment it crosses the boundary back into the model's context, whether or not the tool was read-only.

questions.objective: Locate the trust boundaries between host, client, server, and the tools a server exposes
questions.prompt: A candidate is told a server runs as a separate process from the host. What should they assume about trust by default, absent a specific design that says otherwise?
options: That trust boundaries only apply to servers exposing resources, never to servers exposing tools
That the process boundary also marks a trust boundary, since the server is frequently written or operated by a different party
That the server automatically inherits the host's full trust the moment the handshake completes successfully
That trust is unrelated to process boundaries and depends only on which programming language the server is written in, a detail no part of the specification actually states
questions.explanation: Because the process boundary and the trust boundary usually coincide in practice, the default assumption absent a specific design stating otherwise is that a separately running server is not automatically as trusted as the host that connects to it.

questions.objective: Locate the trust boundaries between host, client, server, and the tools a server exposes
questions.prompt: Which two components sit inside the user's own trust domain, on the same side of the boundary as the host? Select two.
options: The host application itself, which the user runs directly
The tool result content that the server sends back
The client that the host embeds and owns the connection
The server that the client connects to on the other side
questions.explanation: The host and the clients it embeds are components the user's own application controls and are treated as inside the trust domain, while the server and the content it returns sit on the other side of the boundary as external and untrusted by default.

questions.objective: Apply permissions and consent so a user approves what a server may see and do
questions.prompt: A tool only looks something up and reports back, with no effect outside the conversation. What consent treatment does that tool typically receive?
options: It always requires explicit user approval before every single call, the same as a side-effecting tool
It is blocked entirely, since only side-effecting tools are permitted to run at all
A host may let it run without stopping to ask, since it is read-only and changes nothing outside the conversation
It requires approval only the very first time, and never again for any tool afterward, side-effecting or not, which conflicts with the roles this domain defines
questions.explanation: A read-only tool reports on the world without changing it, so a host can let it proceed without a fresh approval, unlike a side-effecting tool, which changes something outside the conversation and requires a real consent decision.

questions.objective: Apply permissions and consent so a user approves what a server may see and do
questions.prompt: A user grants consent for a server's delete_file tool. Does that grant also cover the same server's send_email tool?
options: Yes, but only if both tools are marked read-only in the server's discovery response
Yes, because consent granted for any tool on a server automatically covers every other tool on that server, though the blueprint does not describe it this way
No, but only because the two tools happen to belong to different servers in this example
No, because consent is scoped to the specific tool it was granted for, not to the server as a whole
questions.explanation: Consent is scoped to exactly the tool it was granted for, so approving one side-effecting tool never authorizes a different one to run unattended, even when both tools belong to the same connected server.

questions.objective: Apply permissions and consent so a user approves what a server may see and do
questions.prompt: A host design offers the user a single choice, trust this server, and after that every tool the server exposes runs without any further prompt. What is the main problem with this design?
options: It collapses a specific, informed decision about one tool into a general one the user never actually made
It is not a problem at all, since a server the user already trusts should be allowed unrestricted access
It only fails for read-only tools, since side-effecting tools are unaffected by how broadly consent is scoped
It fails only because it requires too many prompts, overwhelming the user with excessive approval requests
questions.explanation: A blanket per-server trust grant turns individually named, informed decisions into one broad decision the user never actually made about each specific tool, which is the opposite failure from prompt fatigue and remains a problem regardless of how few prompts it produces.

questions.objective: Apply permissions and consent so a user approves what a server may see and do
questions.prompt: Which two design failures does a well-scoped, per-tool consent system avoid? Select two.
options: Keeping a durable record of which tool calls actually ran
Treating every tool call as pre-approved the instant a server connects
Reading a tool's description before deciding whether to expose it to the model at all
Prompting for approval so often, even on read-only calls, that users click through without reading
questions.explanation: Pre-approving every call at connection time and prompting so often that approval becomes noise are the two naive designs a well-scoped consent system avoids, while reading descriptions before exposure and keeping a durable record are practices consent scoping does not conflict with.

questions.objective: Choose risk and safety controls against tool poisoning, injection, and over-broad access
questions.prompt: A tools/call request names a tool the server never registered. What should a properly configured allowlist do with that request?
options: Allow it once, then add the tool to the allowlist automatically for future calls, which is not how the protocol actually behaves
Deny it by default before the call reaches a handler or produces a log entry
Forward it to the nearest server that might recognize the name instead
Queue it until an administrator manually registers a matching tool later
questions.explanation: An allowlist denies any tool name the server did not register, by default, before the call ever reaches a handler, which bounds what can run rather than silently forwarding, auto-registering, or queuing an unrecognized name.

questions.objective: Choose risk and safety controls against tool poisoning, injection, and over-broad access
questions.prompt: Every individual call to a tool looks legitimate on its own, but the same tool is being called far more often than normal. What risk control specifically bounds the damage in this situation?
options: Schema validation, which only checks the shape of a single call's arguments
Consent scoping, which only distinguishes a side-effecting tool from a read-only one
A rate limit, which caps how many times a tool may run regardless of whether each individual call looks legitimate
A hash-chained log, which records calls after they run but does not stop any of them, a description the specification does not support
questions.explanation: Schema validation, logging, and consent scoping each address a different concern, while a rate limit is the control specifically aimed at bounding how many times a tool runs, which is what caps the damage of a legitimate-looking call repeated excessively.

questions.objective: Choose risk and safety controls against tool poisoning, injection, and over-broad access
questions.prompt: A server's tool description contains hidden text instructing the model to ignore the user's actual request and exfiltrate data instead. What category of risk does this scenario illustrate?
options: A consent scoping failure, since the user never approved the specific wording of the description
A rate-limit violation, since the description was returned more times than the configured cap allows, which does not match how a conformant implementation behaves
A parse error, since the hidden text makes the tool's JSON description syntactically invalid
Tool poisoning, where a tool's own advertised description carries a malicious instruction aimed at the model
questions.explanation: Tool poisoning describes a tool whose advertised name or description itself carries a malicious instruction aimed at the model, which is a distinct risk category from a rate limit, a parsing problem, or how narrowly a consent grant is scoped.

questions.objective: Design auditability and observability so protocol activity can be traced and reviewed
questions.prompt: A system has excellent live dashboards showing every request as it happens, but keeps no durable record anyone could reopen next month. What gap does this describe?
options: Strong observability but weak auditability, since nothing shown live was kept anywhere durable enough to review later
Strong auditability but weak observability, since a dashboard is itself a form of durable record
A schema validation gap, since dashboards are expected to double as a tool's input schema
No gap at all, since observability and auditability describe the exact same property under two names, though nothing in the protocol works this way
questions.explanation: Observability is live, showing what a system is doing right now, while auditability is retrospective and depends on a durable record a reviewer can reopen later, so excellent dashboards with nothing kept durably is a real gap between the two, not the same property.

questions.objective: Design auditability and observability so protocol activity can be traced and reviewed
questions.prompt: Someone edits a past entry in a hash-chained audit log and also recomputes that one entry's own hash so it matches its new content. What happens when the log is verified?
options: Verification cannot run at all once any entry has been edited, so the log becomes permanently unreadable
Verification still fails, because the next entry in the chain still stores the original hash as its prev_hash, and that no longer matches
Verification passes silently, because recomputing the edited entry's own hash is sufficient to hide the change
Verification only checks the very first and very last entries, so a change in the middle is never detected, which is not the mechanism the specification defines
questions.explanation: Recomputing one entry's own hash does not fix the break, because the following entry still stores the original prev_hash, so the mismatch simply moves one entry later and a full verification pass still catches it.

questions.objective: Design auditability and observability so protocol activity can be traced and reviewed
questions.prompt: A tool call includes a password argument, and the exchange is being recorded end to end the way a full audited exchange is expected to run. Which two statements correctly describe how that argument should be handled in the record? Select two.
options: The flagged field is replaced with a fixed marker before the entry is ever written or hashed, the detail a conformant design has to get right
The real value is written to the log in the clear first and redacted afterward in a later pass
The entire call is skipped and no log entry is created at all, since sensitive arguments cannot be logged
The tool handler itself still receives the real value, since it needs it to do the actual work
questions.explanation: Redaction replaces a flagged field with a fixed marker before an entry exists in any form, while the handler still receives the real value to do its work, and an audited exchange still records the call rather than skipping logging or redacting only after the value was already written in the clear.

questions.objective: Map the roles, responsibilities, and adoption patterns of teams deploying MCP
questions.prompt: In a deployed MCP system, what is the server author specifically responsible for deciding?
options: Which model the host uses to decide when to call a tool in the first place
How a returned result is rendered on screen, such as a chat bubble or a sidebar panel, which the specification never actually guarantees
Which capabilities exist, such as which tools are registered and what each tool's input schema requires
Which consent flow the host presents to the user before a side-effecting call runs
questions.explanation: A server author decides what capabilities exist, including which tools are registered and what their schemas require, while presentation, consent flow, and model choice are responsibilities that belong to the host rather than to the server's author.

questions.objective: Map the roles, responsibilities, and adoption patterns of teams deploying MCP
questions.prompt: Which of the following is squarely the host's responsibility rather than the server author's?
options: Deciding which fields a specific tool's input schema marks as required
Naming the tools a specific server exposes during discovery
Writing the handler logic that actually executes when a specific tool is called, though this is not how a conformant server or host is expected to act
Owning the consent flow a user sees before a side-effecting tool call is allowed to run
questions.explanation: The host owns how a discovered tool is surfaced to the user, including the consent flow before a call runs, while schema design, handler logic, and tool naming are decisions the server author makes when building the server.

questions.objective: Map the roles, responsibilities, and adoption patterns of teams deploying MCP
questions.prompt: What decision sits with the user, above both the host and the server, in a running deployment?
options: Which of a connected server's capabilities are actually allowed to run, through whatever consent flow the host offers
Which JSON-RPC error code a malformed request should return
Which fields a tool's input schema marks as required versus optional
Which programming language the server author used to implement each tool's handler, which is inconsistent with how the exchange is actually structured
questions.explanation: The user sits above the host and server in the sense that they decide, through the host's consent flow, which of a server's capabilities are actually permitted to run, while implementation language and schema design remain the server author's decisions.

questions.objective: Map the roles, responsibilities, and adoption patterns of teams deploying MCP
questions.prompt: A team that already has one working host wants to adopt a second one for a different team internally. Whose cost is adding that second host, under the roles this domain describes?
options: The end user's cost, since each user must personally reconfigure every server by hand for the new host
The new host vendor's cost, since they write the client-side implementation once, not a cost the existing server author pays again
Nobody's cost, since adopting a second host requires no implementation work from any party involved
The existing server author's cost, since every server must be individually rewritten for each new host that adopts it, a detail no part of the specification actually states
questions.explanation: Because the wire contract is fixed by the specification rather than by any one host, adding a second host is a client-side integration cost the new host's vendor pays once, and it is not a cost the existing server author has to pay again for each host adopted.

questions.objective: Select operational use cases where MCP connects agents to real systems
questions.prompt: A team stands up a server that exposes search over an internal issue tracker. Which description best fits this as an operational use case?
options: A presentation change only, since search results are rendered differently by every host that calls it
A capability limited to exactly one host, since search servers cannot be reused across hosts by design
Connecting internal data to any conformant host, so every team's host can search the same tracker without a separate integration
A one-time migration task that has no ongoing relationship to any host once the server is deployed, which conflicts with the roles this domain defines
questions.explanation: Exposing an issue tracker's search behind a server is a concrete operational use case, connecting internal data to whichever conformant hosts a team adopts, rather than a one-time migration, a presentation concern, or something limited to one host by design.

questions.objective: Select operational use cases where MCP connects agents to real systems
questions.prompt: A server exposes a tool that triggers a multi-step internal approval workflow. What makes this an operational use case in the sense this domain covers?
options: It stops being a use case the moment more than one host is able to reach the same server
It qualifies only if the workflow tool is marked read-only, since side-effecting tools do not count as use cases, though the blueprint does not describe it this way
It only qualifies once the workflow has been rewritten separately for every host that might call it
It connects an agent host to a real internal system that carries out actual work, not just returns descriptive text
questions.explanation: An operational use case connects an agent host to a real system that does actual work, such as a multi-step approval workflow, and being reachable from more than one host through a shared server is the point of the use case, not a disqualifier.

questions.objective: Select operational use cases where MCP connects agents to real systems
questions.prompt: A server exposes a tool that triggers a production deployment. Given how this domain frames operational use cases, what should be true of this specific tool at the consent layer?
options: It should be treated as side-effecting and gated behind explicit consent, since it changes something real outside the conversation
It should bypass consent entirely, since deploy tools are assumed safe by every host automatically
It should be treated as read-only, since triggering a deployment only reports on the current state of the system, which is not how the protocol actually behaves
It should be excluded from discovery entirely, since destructive tools cannot be exposed through MCP at all
questions.explanation: A tool that triggers a real deployment changes something outside the conversation, which places it in the side-effecting category that a conformant host gates behind explicit consent rather than exposing as read-only, exempt, or hidden from discovery.

questions.objective: Select operational use cases where MCP connects agents to real systems
questions.prompt: A team wants a host to answer general knowledge questions with no connection to any internal system at all. Is standing up an MCP server a fitting operational use case for that specific need?
options: Yes, because every single host interaction must be routed through some MCP server before it can proceed, regardless of whether an external system is involved at all
Not particularly, since operational use cases connect a host to real internal data, tools, or workflows, not general knowledge with no external system involved
Not particularly, but only because general knowledge questions are technically impossible for any tool to ever answer correctly
Yes, because a tool must exist before a model is able to produce any text response at all, even a purely conversational one
questions.explanation: The operational use cases this domain covers are about connecting a host to real internal data, tools, or workflows, so a need with no external system involved at all does not call for a server the way a ticket search or a deploy trigger does.

questions.objective: Reason about ecosystem and portability across MCP clients, servers, gateways, and registries
questions.prompt: What specifically allows an unmodified server to work correctly when a brand-new host adopts it, without the server author changing anything?
options: The server maintains a private list of every host it has ever seen and adjusts its answers per host
A translation layer sitting between the host and the server converts each host's dialect into the server's own format, a description the specification does not support
The server answers the fixed wire contract the same way regardless of which client sent the request, with no host-specific branching in its own code
The new host automatically rewrites the server's code the first time it connects to it
questions.explanation: Portability comes from the server answering the same fixed wire contract identically no matter which client sent the request, with no branch of logic keyed to a specific host, rather than from a translation layer or host-specific code paths inside the server.

questions.objective: Reason about ecosystem and portability across MCP clients, servers, gateways, and registries
questions.prompt: Two different hosts call the same tool on the same server with identical arguments. What is each host free to do differently, without breaking portability?
options: Silently change the tool's name before displaying it, so users of each host see two unrelated tool names, which does not match how a conformant implementation behaves
Skip schema validation entirely, since validation is understood to be optional for exactly one of the two hosts
Return a different result payload for the exact same tool name and arguments
Render the returned result differently on screen and apply its own consent flow and sampling policy around the call
questions.explanation: What travels unchanged across hosts is the capability contract, meaning the tool names, schemas, and result payload, while presentation, consent flow, and sampling policy are host-side concerns each host is free to handle its own way without breaking portability.

questions.objective: Reason about ecosystem and portability across MCP clients, servers, gateways, and registries
questions.prompt: A team wants to discover and reach many independently operated MCP servers without hard-coding a connection to each one by hand. Which ecosystem concept is built for exactly that role?
options: A registry or a gateway, which extends the same portability property across many servers at once
A notification, since notifications are the only message type capable of naming more than one server
A second host, since only a host is capable of discovering more than one server
A tool's inputSchema, since schemas are what list every server currently available on a network
questions.explanation: A registry or gateway is the ecosystem concept built to let a client discover and reach many independently operated servers without hand-coding each connection, extending the same wire-contract portability across a larger set of servers at once.

questions.objective: Reason about ecosystem and portability across MCP clients, servers, gateways, and registries
questions.prompt: Which two things are guaranteed to stay identical across every conformant host that calls the same tool with the same arguments? Select two.
options: The specific consent prompt wording the host shows before the call runs
The tool's name and its input schema
The result payload the call returns, matching how the exchange is actually structured
The exact visual layout used to render the result on screen
questions.explanation: The capability contract, meaning the tool's name, schema, and the payload a call returns, stays identical no matter which conformant host calls it, while rendering and consent prompt wording are host-side presentation choices that are not part of that guarantee.
